body:
Hi, thanks for reporting!

What you're experiencing is (I think) the danger of nontrivial relocatability. I have gone into detail for this problem here:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/100509

In short, relocation is practically copying the data, and then deallocating the old data without destructing it. 
This is safe for almost all types, except those that have pointers into itself.

Since these kinds of types are rare, and can usually be re-written to use relative pointers to themselves instead, we have chosen to assume trivial relocatability for _all_ of Godot's types. This is why `LocalVector` is not calling your dtor on `resize`.

> I think LocalVector assumes it can do a bitwise-copy of the data when doing a memrealloc (e.g. on resize/reserve). If realloc manages to extend the current memory block, then I think it's fine. But if realloc needs to use a completely new memory block, then it will bitwise-copy current data, which is not correct if the type is not trivially copyable. So we would probably need to use placement new with copy/move ctor on non-trivially copyable/movable types.

This is where it's relevant - `LocalVector` doesn't actually _copy_ the old data - it _relocates_ it. 

As indicated above, I recommend introspecting your types if you can make them trivially relocatable. I'm happy to help if you run into trouble :)

Oh, I see! Then, it must be that I'm using types that are non trivially relocatable.
(I added an ```std::function``` to an existing engine type, which was used in a ```LocalVector```, and then it started crashing).
My case is very rare and custom, so the assumption makes a lot of sense for 99% of ```LocalVector``` usages.
I'll just be careful from now on then, taking this into account!
Thanks for the detailed explanation 😌
